s: Content-based laws target speech based on its communicative content: its topic, idea or message.
They are presumptively unconstitutional and must satisfy strict scrutiny, meaning narrow tailoring to a compelling interest by the least restrictive means (Reed v. Town of Gilbert, 2015).
A law is content-based on its face if it defines regulated speech by subject matter or by function or purpose.
A facially neutral law is content-based if it cannot be justified without reference to content or was adopted because of disagreement with the message.
Location-based sign rules are content-neutral even if they require reading the sign (City of Austin v. Reagan National Advertising, 2022).
Viewpoint discrimination is the most egregious form and is nearly always invalid, even in nonpublic forums and for trademarks (Matal v. Tam, 2017; Iancu v. Brunetti, 2019; Rosenberger, 1995).

Content-neutral time, place and manner rules are valid if they are narrowly tailored to a significant government interest and leave open ample alternative channels (Ward v. Rock Against Racism, 1989).
Narrow tailoring here does not require the least restrictive means, only that the law not burden substantially more speech than necessary.
McCullen v. Coakley (2014) struck down a thirty-five-foot abortion-clinic buffer zone as insufficiently tailored.
